items.prompt: The original route wrote body as { ingredients: unknown; ... }. A client posts the JSON literal null. What did the assertion do about it?
items.answer: Nothing - an assertion only tells the compiler how to treat the expression; the revised parser's record() guard is what rejects null at runtime
distractors: It threw a TypeError because null does not match the asserted shape
It converted null into an empty object with undefined fields
Next.js rejected the request before the handler ran
items.explanation: A TypeScript assertion does not inspect the value. The parser accepts unknown and establishes properties before returning typed values.

items.prompt: A request arrives with servings as the string "2". How many paid provider calls does generateRecipeResponse make?
items.answer: Zero - parseGenerationInput runs before the retry loop and the route returns 400
distractors: One - the provider is asked once, then the output fails validation
Two - both attempts run because the retry loop catches every error
One - the string is coerced to 2 and generation succeeds
items.explanation: Placing parsing before the retry loop means retrying can never turn invalid input into a paid request - correctness and cost control at once.

items.prompt: Which normalisation does the parser perform on accepted values?
items.answer: Only trimming of text; numbers must already be finite numbers, so "2" is rejected rather than converted
distractors: It trims text and parses numeric strings into numbers
It lowercases every string so comparisons are case-insensitive
None at all; values are returned exactly as received
items.explanation: text() returns the trimmed value; number() rejects strings, NaN and Infinity.

items.prompt: A request lists ingredients [" Rice", "rice "]. What is the response?
items.answer: 400 'Ingredients must be distinct.' - text() trims both and the distinctness check compares lowercased values
distractors: 200, because the raw strings differ
200 with one rice ingredient after deduplication
400 'Ingredient must be non-empty text' because of the whitespace
items.explanation: Trim, then lowercase for the Set comparison: two spellings of one ingredient are rejected, not silently merged.

items.prompt: A request includes an extra field injected: "ignored". Does it reach the provider?
items.answer: No - parseGenerationInput builds a new object from named fields only, and the test asserts the provider saw exactly the normalized input
distractors: Yes - unknown fields pass through untouched
No - the request is rejected with 400 for unexpected fields
Yes - but it is removed later by parseRecipes
items.explanation: Constructing the output from named fields drops anything else by construction.

items.prompt: The request asks for 30 minutes and 2 servings. The provider returns three well-formed recipes, one taking 45 minutes. What happens?
items.answer: parseRecipes throws 'Recipes must respect the requested time and servings.', so that attempt fails and the orchestrator may retry
distractors: The 45-minute recipe is dropped and two recipes are returned
All three are returned because each recipe is individually valid
The 45-minute recipe's time is clamped to 30
items.explanation: Cross-field rules only run when the caller passes the accepted input; they check fit, not just shape.

items.prompt: The provider returns unparseable output twice in a row. What does the browser receive?
items.answer: A 500 with a generic 'Couldn't generate recipes right now' message - provider details are never copied into the response
distractors: A 500 containing the parser's specific error message
A 502 with the raw provider response for debugging
A 200 with an empty recipes array
items.explanation: Model output is nondeterministic, so one retry may help; after two failures the response stays generic.

items.prompt: Saved history contains four entries, two of them malformed. What does reading it return, and is storage changed?
items.answer: The two valid entries; the bad ones are dropped individually and the stored string is not rewritten during the read
distractors: An empty list, because one bad entry invalidates the collection
The two valid entries, and storage is rewritten without the bad ones
All four, with the malformed ones marked as corrupt
items.explanation: History is a collection of independent records, so partial recovery is useful - and reads must not perform destructive cleanup.

items.prompt: Why does a provider response with one bad recipe fail entirely, while history with one bad entry recovers partially?
items.answer: A provider response is one new collection that must satisfy the whole contract; history is independent records the user owns, so dropping only the bad one is useful
distractors: Because provider errors are cheaper to retry than storage reads
Because localStorage cannot throw, so failure there is impossible
It is an arbitrary style choice between throwing and catching
items.explanation: The policy difference comes from ownership and user expectations, not from a preference for exceptions.

items.prompt: A vegan request returns recipes containing butter marked isFromUser: true. Does the parser catch it?
items.answer: No - it verifies shape and arithmetic, not truth: neither dietary compliance nor that isFromUser ingredients appear in the user's list is checked
distractors: Yes - dietary preferences are cross-checked against ingredient names
Yes - isFromUser ingredients are matched against the request list
Only if allowMissingOne is false
items.explanation: Do not turn a successful parser result into a stronger product claim than its code supports.

items.prompt: A crafted share link decodes to {"title":"x"}. What happens on the shared-recipe page?
items.answer: decodeRecipe returns it via JSON.parse(...) as Recipe without validation, and rendering crashes at recipe.ingredients.map
distractors: decodeRecipe returns null and the page shows 'recipe not found'
parseRecipe rejects it and the page redirects home
The missing fields default to empty arrays and the page renders
items.explanation: The fix wraps the parse in parseRecipe inside the existing try, so the catch returns null for invalid links.

items.prompt: Why does the in-memory rate limiter limit honest users but not attackers?
items.answer: It keys on the client-controlled x-forwarded-for header, so an attacker rotates values; the Map never evicts and is per-instance on serverless
distractors: It counts requests per minute but resets on every successful call
It only applies to GET requests while generation uses POST
It limits by API key, which attackers do not send
items.explanation: Rated Medium because each bypassed request can cost a paid provider call.

items.front: Name the three contracts the parser distinguishes (request contract in lib/validation.ts:39-67) and what each checks.
items.back: Request: 2-20 distinct ingredient strings, a time limit of 15/30/45/60, 1-6 whole servings, supported dietary options, skill choice, real boolean. Recipe: nested objects, positive finite amounts, bounded text, consecutive step order. Collection: exactly three distinct ids, time/servings/missing-ingredient consistent with the accepted request.

items.front: The four parser primitives in lib/validation.ts:10-37 - what does each accept?
items.back: record: plain objects (not null, arrays, primitives). text: non-blank strings up to a trimmed maximum, returns the trimmed value. number: finite numbers in [min, max], optionally integers. list: arrays with length in [min, max].

items.front: Recipe ids are checked distinct only within a batch (lib/validation.ts:109). Why is that a bug for favourites, and where is the clean fix?
items.back: Favourites are keyed by id globally, so two batches can reuse an id and toggling one recipe un-favourites another. Fix on the server right after parseRecipes succeeds in lib/generation.ts: replace each id with crypto.randomUUID() so every consumer sees globally unique ids.

items.front: Finding 5: lib/generation.ts:24-26 catches every provider/parse error silently. What is the operability cost, and what should a fix add without leaking details?
items.back: A missing API key is indistinguishable from bad output. Log an internal event with a correlation id, attempt number and a bounded category (parse_failure, transport_failure) while keeping the public response generic - test that a distinctive private message is absent from the response.
